A spree is a short burst of time during which a person does one particular thing repeatedly, intensely, and with very little restraint — often more than they normally would. Think of it as a temporary loss of control over a specific urge or behaviour.

The two most important ideas packed into this word are:

  • Intensity — a lot of the same thing happening at once
  • Brevity — it doesn't last forever; it's a concentrated episode, not a lifestyle

Not every activity qualifies. For the word "spree" to fit, the situation usually has these qualities:

1. It involves repetition of one act.
You're not doing many different things. You're doing one thing over and over — buying, eating, spending, committing crimes, etc.

2. It's excessive.
The amount or frequency goes beyond what is considered normal or reasonable. A person buying one shirt is not a spree. A person buying twenty things in one afternoon — that's a spree.

3. It feels driven or uncontrolled.
There's a sense that the person has given in to an urge or is swept up in the moment. Even if the person is consciously choosing to indulge, the word "spree" suggests they've temporarily thrown their usual caution or restraint aside.

4. It's temporary.
A spree has a beginning and an end. It is an episode, not a permanent pattern of behaviour. Someone who always overspends is not "on a spree" — they just have a habit. But someone who suddenly blows all their savings in a weekend? That's a spree.
The Word Is Neutral — Context Decides the Tone

This is very important: the word "spree" on its own carries no inherently good or bad meaning. It is simply a label for this kind of intense, concentrated episode.

What makes it sound fun and lighthearted — or dark and disturbing — is what comes before it.

Compare:

  • A shopping spree sounds exciting, even joyful. You picture someone walking through a mall with bags in both hands, laughing, buying whatever they want.
  • A killing spree sounds horrifying. You picture violence, chaos, tragedy.

Same structure. Same word. The meaning of the full phrase depends entirely on the action described.

The word "spree" is almost always paired with the type of activity. Here are the most frequently used ones:

  • Shopping spree — buying many things in a short period, usually impulsively or extravagantly
  • Spending spree — similar to shopping spree, but the focus is on the money being spent rather than the act of shopping itself; can apply to any kind of spending, not just in shops
  • Eating spree / binge — consuming large amounts of food in one go
  • Drinking spree — consuming excessive alcohol over a short period
  • Crime spree — a series of crimes committed by the same person or group within a short stretch of time (e.g. a burglar who breaks into ten houses in one week)
  • Killing spree — a series of murders committed rapidly, often in a single episode of violence
  • Building spree / construction spree — rapid, large-scale construction happening in a short period (used in news and journalism: "The city went on a building spree in the 1990s.")
  • Signing spree — used in sports, when a team signs many new players in a short window of time

Notice that the first word (shopping, crime, killing, etc.) tells you what is being done excessively. "Spree" just tells you how — rapidly, repeatedly, with abandon.
The Phrases: "On a Spree" and "Go on a Spree"

These are the most natural ways to use the word in a sentence.

"On a spree" means someone is currently in the middle of this burst of activity:

  • "She's been on a shopping spree all afternoon."
  • "The criminal was on a spree across three cities."

"Go on a spree" means to begin or embark on this burst of activity:

  • "He got his bonus and went on a spending spree."
  • "Let's go on a shopping spree this weekend!"

You can also say someone "went on a spree" (past tense) to describe something that already happened:

  • "After months of saving, they went on a shopping spree and bought everything they had been eyeing."
How Formal or Informal Is It?

"Spree" is a fairly informal word. You'll hear it in everyday speech, in newspaper headlines, and in casual writing. It is not a formal or academic word. That said, it is completely standard — there is nothing slang-like or inappropriate about it. It appears in formal journalism too, particularly in phrases like "crime spree" or "spending spree."

These will help you see the word alive in natural context:

  1. "The kids went on an eating spree at the birthday party and had cake, chips, and candy all afternoon."
  2. "The police were trying to catch the thief who had been on a crime spree, robbing five shops in three days."
  3. "I told myself I'd buy just one thing, but I ended up on a full-blown shopping spree and spent way more than I planned."
  4. "The government went on a hiring spree, recruiting thousands of new workers within just a few months."
  5. "After the band released their new album, they went on a press spree, appearing on every major TV show and podcast."

To avoid misusing the word, here's what it doesn't mean:

  • It does not mean a single, isolated act. Buying one expensive item is not a "spree."
  • It does not describe a long, slow pattern. Gradual overspending over years is not a "spree."
  • It does not apply to doing many different things. A busy weekend where you clean the house, see a friend, and cook a meal is not a "spree" of any kind.

The key is always: one type of action, done many times over, in a short and intense burst.

A spree is a concentrated, often impulsive episode of doing one thing repeatedly and excessively, in a short period of time. It can describe something fun (a shopping spree) or something terrible (a crime spree). The word itself is neutral — the action paired with it gives it its emotional colour. It almost always appears in the patterns "a _ spree", "on a _ spree", or "go on a _ spree".
